title: ChatGPT Gets an A+: What That Means for Law School, Workflows, and Your Everyday Life — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source accepts that foundational legal understanding remains necessary for effective AI collaboration and materially extends the cluster’s proposed response upstream into law-school teaching and assessment. It advocates training students in collaborative, critical AI workflows from the outset, while questioning whether traditional closed-book methods are the best way to reproduce expertise. Its claims are proposals and predictions, not evidence that these reforms produce equivalent practice competence.
qs: Without understanding the architecture, even if you have the super-intelligent AI hologram next to you, you won’t be able to work well with your AI hologram to help it help you with a client’s problem.
So let’s start training for what’s obviously coming next, which is going to be some workflow where we’re working together with the technology.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts selective, lawyer-in-the-loop augmentation by insisting that lawyers retain foundational legal understanding and actively question AI outputs. It materially extends the cluster by proposing early AI-collaborative education and redesigned assessment to prepare future lawyers for those workflows, while treating improved outcomes as a prediction rather than established practice evidence.
qs: Without understanding the architecture, even if you have the super-intelligent AI hologram next to you, you won’t be able to work well with your AI hologram to help it help you with a client’s problem.
So let’s start training for what’s obviously coming next, which is going to be some workflow where we’re working together with the technology.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, human-led deployment and materially extends the cluster by showing that indiscriminate context loading can degrade performance, while proposing a staged maturity model for moving from experimentation through workflow integration to organisational transformation. It also links effective AI use to lawyers’ continuing understanding of legal architecture.
qs: They hypothesized that the model would perform better, but actually it performed worse than when it simply had access to the case law and the syllabus.

(As you know, I’ve thought a lot about this at the AAA, from experimentation to point solutions to integration in workflows to full transformation.) And then for each of those stages, what are the use cases, what are the enablers, what are the risks you’re going to worry about, the barriers that are going to make it hard to get to the next stage, and then what’s the sign that you’ll be ready for the next stage?

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s coordinated-development proposition by calling for law firms, law schools and other stakeholders to overcome silos, test new approaches and share results. It treats reform as an uncertain, iterative process rather than claiming that a settled or validated model already exists.
qs: I don’t know that they talk to each other enough to figure out the kind of collaborative solution that I think our profession needs at this time.

I think we need to start really understanding and trying and testing and taking new approaches – and like you said, sharing across silos what we’re learning and what we need more of and what’s working and what’s not.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s practitioner-experimentation proposition through reported routine use of AI for workshops, presentations and unfamiliar work, while also identifying stale memory as a practical limitation. Its evidence is experiential rather than comparative and does not materially extend the cluster’s redesign, governance or reliability agenda.
qs: As somebody who does workshops all the time – and before that, taught classes that were really experimental – I think it is the best for helping you design activities for different groups and coming up with even just the timing.
And I’ve since forgotten that I even saw it or asked it, but it constantly sort of brings it up.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s training-redesign proposition: foundational legal understanding remains necessary for effective AI-assisted practice, while traditional memorisation-based assessment should be reconsidered. It offers conceptual support rather than a concrete replacement model or empirical evidence.
qs: Without understanding the architecture, even if you have the super-intelligent AI hologram next to you, you won’t be able to work well with your AI hologram to help it help you with a client’s problem.
I don’t know that we can’t do better than a “memorize it all, closed-book test, issue-spotting” way to be confident that lawyers understand that architecture – that feels shortsighted to me.

kp.k: Reasoning models reportedly achieve top law-school exam grades
kp.d: Leonard reports a University of Maryland law-school study tracking successive ChatGPT versions on professors’ exams. She says earlier GPT-3 and GPT-4 trials produced mostly C’s and B’s, whereas O3 received three A+ grades, one A, one A–, two B+ grades, and one B. McCormack says the A+ performances matched or exceeded the top student and emphasizes that O3 is a general frontier model, not a legal-specific product. These are the hosts’ accounts of the study, rather than independently presented study data.
qs: As I mentioned, O3 got three A+ grades, one A, one A–, two B+ grades, and one B.
This has been a huge improvement over the first few trials they ran with GPT-3 and GPT-4, where the models received mostly C’s and B’s.
From the study, the courses it got an A+ in – it performed as well as or better than the very top student.

kp.k: Exam outcomes depend on currency and prompting
kp.d: Leonard attributes O3’s B in Administrative Law to a training cutoff preceding Loper Bright’s overturning of Chevron, and a B+ in Secured Transactions to researchers omitting answer-format instructions. Her confidence that current case access would have produced an A or A+ in Administrative Law is a counterfactual prediction, not a reported retest result.
qs: The reason O3 got a B in Admin is because its training data cut off before the Loper Bright case
So, if it had actually had access to the most relevant recent case, I’m sure it would have also performed in the A or A+ level.
The researchers didn’t prompt the model correctly, and they failed to give it the instructions on how the answers should have been formatted.

kp.k: Adding legal context can worsen model performance
kp.d: Leonard reports that a Torts retest supplying about 70,000 words of professor’s notes performed worse than the case-law-and-syllabus condition, contrary to the researchers’ hypothesis. McCormack supplies a related organizational observation: internal dispute-area handbooks, especially with multi-agent models, have yielded high performance, but adding background case law has degraded it. The latter is an unquantified practitioner account.
qs: They hypothesized that the model would perform better, but actually it performed worse than when it simply had access to the case law and the syllabus.

First of all, we have found that when we build with our internal handbook of knowledge about, say, a particular dispute area, we’re seeing – especially when we build a multi-agent model – really high performance.
But if you add basically a bunch of background case law in that area, it degrades – it’s worse.

kp.k: AI performance challenges conventional law-school assessment
kp.d: Both hosts question the value of semester-end, closed-book issue-spotting examinations when AI can excel at them and lawyers in practice can consult sources. Leonard leaves unresolved whether independent issue-spotting and doctrinal application remain essential foundations or principally exercises in lawyer formation. She frames cheating as less important than what the assessment measures, citing her belief that students generally follow rules and can be disconnected from AI.
qs: There have been critiques of the law school teaching style of a semester-long class with one assessment at the end (that’s a closed-book assessment – something that doesn’t happen in legal practice).

Maybe the argument that says it still matters is that this is foundational, and even if machines can do it better than students, it’s still a part of forming your ability as a lawyer to be able to understand the law and why your client’s situation means something in the context of that legal framework.
Does it only matter for the development of a lawyer’s mind, or does it actually have any real value in practice once the machine can actually do this?

kp.k: Teach legal foundations alongside human–AI collaboration
kp.d: McCormack argues that lawyers still need the architecture of law—sources, public and private law, rights and remedies—to work effectively with AI on client problems. She proposes exploring AI-assisted learning and collaborative issue-spotting rather than treating memorization-based examinations as indispensable. Her expectation of better legal outcomes with AI is explicitly a guess, supported by analogy to medical studies she mentions without identifying them.
qs: Without understanding the architecture, even if you have the super-intelligent AI hologram next to you, you won’t be able to work well with your AI hologram to help it help you with a client’s problem.
Maybe it’s using your AI partner from the beginning to help you spot the issues and work together on what they are.
And my guess is we’re going to get better outcomes now that they’re getting A+’s, if we work with them, than without them.

kp.k: AI puts recruitment signals under pressure
kp.d: Leonard argues that AI’s ability to obtain high exam grades and draft Law Review comments should prompt employers to reconsider prestige, grades and journal credentials as indicators of client-valued capability. She reports discussions with Andy Perlman that employers request tech-enabled graduates but continue rewarding institutional brand. McCormack qualifies the argument: traditional credentials were signals of potential rather than direct proof of practice success. Neither identifies a settled replacement selection system.
qs: the market constantly says that it wants tech-enabled law students and graduates, but it doesn’t reward the schools that actually prioritize that – it rewards prestige and brand.
So, if you’re an employer, doesn’t everything start to break down around the way that you think about recruitment – or shouldn’t it?
I think the grades and the Law Review were just a signal that that person was going to be able to be successful at the highest level of practice.

kp.k: Employers and educators should coordinate experimentation
kp.d: McCormack says hiring organizations must signal demand for additional capabilities and argues that professional stakeholder silos impede collaborative responses. Leonard concludes that the study creates urgency for trying new educational approaches and sharing findings across institutions. Both qualify their knowledge of existing faculty discussions rather than establishing that law schools are inactive.
qs: It’s going to take some signaling from the places that hire law students that they want to see more.
I don’t know that they talk to each other enough to figure out the kind of collaborative solution that I think our profession needs at this time.

I think we need to start really understanding and trying and testing and taking new approaches – and like you said, sharing across silos what we’re learning and what we need more of and what’s working and what’s not.

kp.k: Connectors move AI into everyday legal workflows
kp.d: Leonard describes newly announced, permission-based ChatGPT connections to email, calendars, spreadsheets, CRMs and internal systems, alongside similar Claude integrations. She sees cross-system access as reducing platform switching. For law firms, she highlights Harvey’s announced iManage connection as addressing an impediment to usefulness and interprets the strategy as embedding AI throughout work. McCormack’s proposed weekly reflection, calendar and follow-up system remains an experiment whose results she has not yet reported.
qs: So essentially ChatGPT can – if you give it permission – read and write emails, summarize your calendar events, pull data from spreadsheets or CRMs.
Harvey announced that it was connecting with iManage (which is used by most major law firms for their internal document management systems).
And again, in all of our conversations, that has been a big impediment to having lawyers actually see how useful this can be, because they’ve had to toggle back and forth.

kp.k: Integration raises security and retention concerns
kp.d: Leonard notes security experts’ concerns about connectors and warns that legal proceedings can override providers’ data-handling promises. She cites the reported court-ordered retention of OpenAI material users had been told would be deleted. Separately, the hosts discuss auditing chatbot memory because prompts written for other people or demonstration audiences can distort later personalization; Leonard attributes the audit suggestion to their friend Edson and says she has not yet tried it.
qs: I know there are all sorts of posts and thought pieces from security experts about some of the risks involved here.
you can trust these companies if you choose to, but other legal proceedings might intervene and other things could supersede their promises, even if they are promising not to share your data.
Ed suggested running a “memory audit” and asking ChatGPT to share everything it knows about you, and then tell it to forget certain things

kp.k: Practitioner examples show iterative AI augmentation
kp.d: McCormack describes using ChatGPT to design a 60-minute interactive workshop for approximately 250 or 300 diverse participants, repeatedly correcting suggestions for room layout and audience needs. The workshop built an AI maturity matrix spanning experimentation, point solutions, workflow integration and transformation, including risks and progression barriers. She reports completing the matrix and producing a takeaway, while acknowledging good, mediocre and bad AI suggestions; this is anecdotal evidence of augmentation, not measured productivity.
qs: As you know, I’ve thought a lot about this at the AAA, from experimentation to point solutions to integration in workflows to full transformation.
I got so many good ideas, and a lot of mediocre ideas, and some bad ideas
We actually got through the entire matrix, and we had a final product.

kp.k: Exploratory research tolerates different verification requirements
kp.d: Leonard describes using Deep Research to identify potential nonprofit funders and comparable projects, including suggested differentiation arguments. She treats the output as preliminary orientation rather than verified research and says the task did not require complete accuracy. McCormack similarly uses it to identify topics for further investigation. These personal workflow examples distinguish exploratory assistance from uses requiring more rigorous human fact-checking.
qs: But I think this was a great example of a place where I didn’t need 100% accuracy.
I really just needed to get a sense of the lay of the land.
So, I would say that was my AI Aha!, and learning when to use Deep Research and when I need more rigorous fact-checking and that kind of thing.

kp.k: Meta investment illustrates infrastructure competition and consolidation concerns
kp.d: McCormack describes Meta’s $14.8 billion transaction for a 49% Scale AI stake as an effort to improve its AI position through structured-data capabilities and talent, following what she characterizes as disappointing Llama 4 performance. She discusses open-weight distribution as a route to developer workflow embedding but says she cannot determine why the strategy proved insufficient. Leonard reports speculation that the minority stake could avoid antitrust scrutiny and raises concerns about consolidation and talent concentration; she does not present this motive as established.
qs: Maybe because of the price Meta is paying to take a 49% stake in Scale AI. It’s a $14.8 billion transaction.
if more developers are building on your models, you become embedded in more workflows, right?
I’ve heard a lot of conversation about the structure of this investment and the 49% stake, that it could potentially be designed to avoid antitrust scrutiny.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack describe reasoning models as reaching top-student performance on law school examinations.
pts.d: Leonard reports that OpenAI's o3 earned three A+ grades among eight examination grades, improving on earlier models' mostly C and B results. McCormack says the A+ results matched or exceeded the best student. Leonard's suggestion of near-AGI is explicitly limited to the law school examination context, not a finding about autonomous legal practice.

pts.k: Both speakers say adding more legal material can worsen AI performance rather than improve it.
pts.d: Leonard reports worse Torts examination performance after adding approximately 70,000 words of professor notes. McCormack describes a similar effect in internal dispute-area systems: curated handbook knowledge supports high performance, especially with multi-agent models, whereas added background case law can degrade it.

pts.k: Leonard argues that connecting AI to workplace information removes a major barrier to useful legal workflows.
pts.d: She describes general-purpose connectors and Harvey's announced iManage connection as steps toward embedding AI in daily work rather than requiring lawyers to switch between platforms. Harvey is the legal-AI vendor here, not a legal-service provider.

pts.k: The speakers describe present-day AI augmentation of professional planning and exploratory research.
pts.d: McCormack credits iterative ChatGPT assistance with helping design a successful, hour-long workshop for roughly 250–300 diverse participants. Leonard says Deep Research helped identify potential foundations, comparable projects, and ways to distinguish a funding proposal. These are supporting professional workflows, not demonstrated substitution for lawyers.

pts.k: McCormack predicts collaborative lawyer–AI workflows and better outcomes, and calls for training students accordingly.
pts.d: Her better-outcomes claim is explicitly a guess extrapolated from examination performance and an analogy to medical AI studies, not a reported legal-practice outcome study. She advocates augmentation: lawyers must still understand legal sources, rights, remedies, and institutions to work effectively with AI.

pts.k: Leonard suggests AI may undermine traditional recruitment signals; McCormack calls for employer signaling and coordination with law schools.
pts.d: Leonard frames this as a conditional question: if AI can reproduce high examination performance and Law Review writing, employers should reconsider which graduate skills add value clients will pay for. McCormack treats grades and Law Review as historical signals of potential rather than direct guarantees of practice success. Neither presents measured changes in hiring or predicts a quantified employment loss.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The examination claim rests on the speakers' account of a University of Maryland law school study.
pts.d: Leonard describes professors tracking successive ChatGPT models on their examinations. The transcript supplies grades and selected testing conditions, but not a full study citation or comprehensive methodology. These are reported examination results rather than measured client outcomes.

pts.k: The information-overload claim combines a reported examination experiment with McCormack's implementation experience.
pts.d: Leonard also invokes other research without identifying it. McCormack supplies no numerical performance measures or testing protocol for the internal systems. Their analogies to human examination preparation explain their interpretation rather than provide additional experimental evidence.

pts.k: Professional-workflow benefits are based on personal experience and carry quality qualifications.
pts.d: McCormack reports mixed-quality suggestions and active iteration, rather than uncritical reliance. Leonard explicitly limits her favorable research example to orientation where complete accuracy was unnecessary and distinguishes it from work requiring more rigorous human fact-checking.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Leonard identifies legal currency and prompting as conditions affecting examination performance.
pts.d: In this 2025 episode, Leonard attributes the Administrative Law B to a training cutoff preceding Loper Bright and a Secured Transactions B+ to missing answer-format instructions. Her statement that current law would have produced an A or A+ is a counterfactual prediction, not a reported retest result.

pts.k: Connector benefits are presented as emerging capabilities, conditional on access, permission, and information-governance risks.
pts.d: Leonard places the announcements in the preceding week and qualifies her account of account-tier availability. She warns that litigation-related retention duties may override vendor promises. McCormack's connected weekly planning workflow is prospective and not yet a demonstrated productivity result.

pts.k: Educational change is urged soon, while the continuing value of traditional examination skills remains unresolved.
pts.d: Leonard imagines students five years ahead questioning assessments of work machines can already perform. She explicitly leaves open whether issue-spotting and doctrinal application remain necessary foundations. McCormack favors teaching legal architecture and AI collaboration without assuming memorization and closed-book testing are the only ways to do so.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students, educators, legal employers, practicing lawyers, clients, and information-governance teams.
pts.d: Students and educators face questions about curricula, assessment, foundational knowledge, and AI collaboration. Firms and other graduate employers face possible changes to recruitment signals and valued skills. Practicing lawyers, particularly in firms using document-management systems, may gain more integrated workflows. Clients are potential beneficiaries of the better outcomes McCormack predicts, not recipients of measured benefits in this transcript. Information leaders face permission, security, and retention issues as systems connect to organizational data.
